name: The visible world as beautiful, not evil (Plotinus's anti-Gnostic argument)
plain_explanation: Some contemporaries (the Gnostics) held that the physical universe and its Creator are evil, and that only the human soul has any real worth. Plotinus strongly disagreed: he found the physical universe -- the stars, geometric patterns, the beauty of paintings and faces -- genuinely beautiful, a real (if lesser) reflection of the intellectual world above it, and worthy of reverence rather than contempt.
precise_definition: Plotinus's sustained polemic (chiefly in the Second Ennead's 'Tractate on the Gnostics') against the Gnostic doctrine that the created cosmos and its maker are evil; Plotinus argues instead that the world of sense, though inevitably an imperfect copy of the intellectual realm, is 'as good as a sensible world can be,' and that the heavenly bodies in particular are the bodies of god-like beings far superior to human souls, not products of an evil demiurge.
why_it_mattered: This is one of Russell's chief reasons for finding something genuinely attractive and 'beautiful' in Plotinus's mysticism: unlike much later Christian and pagan asceticism (which Russell says came to 'glorify ugliness and dirt'), 'there is in the mysticism of Plotinus nothing morose or hostile to beauty.'
historical_origin: A direct response to contemporary Gnostic teaching, addressed explicitly in Ennead II.9.
examples: Plotinus's rhetorical question: could anyone who loves geometry or music fail to be moved by the harmony and symmetry visible in the physical world?
His argument that the stars and heavens, being 'far purer and lovelier' than human souls, must themselves have some communion with the Immortal Principle, against the Gnostic claim that they do not
objections: Plotinus does concede that some Gnostic elements (such as hatred of matter) may derive legitimately from Plato himself, even while rejecting the rest of Gnostic doctrine as false
competing_positions: Gnosticism, which held the cosmos and its Creator to be evil and only the human soul divine
influence_on_later_thinkers: Russell notes that Julian the Apostate and later Christian ascetics moved toward the opposite, world-denying view Plotinus rejected -- 'beauty... came to be thought of the Devil' -- making Plotinus, in this respect, an end rather than a beginning within the ancient tradition.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly engages a live theological/religious controversy of Plotinus's own time.
